words.sense: Clear and strongly reasoned enough to persuade or withstand objection.
misconceptions: Ignoring strong evidence because the presentation is informal.
Assuming an understandable claim must be well supported.

words.sense: Logically connected and easy to understand, without necessarily being convincing.
misconceptions: Treating clarity and order as proof that an argument is persuasive.
Assuming an understandable claim must be well supported.

semantic_axes.description: Cogent reasoning is persuasive because it is well supported; coherent reasoning is understandable and connected even if its claims are weak.

chains.frame: Which word best describes Malik’s case for changing the lunch menu?

beats.text: Malik compared supplier prices and showed that his proposed lunches would cost less while meeting the same requirements.
beats.decisive_clue: comparative figures justify the proposed change
beats.reason: Comparative figures justify the proposed change. Clear and strongly reasoned enough to persuade or withstand objection.

beats.text: He presented his figures from handwritten notes rather than slides.
beats.decisive_clue: handwritten notes do not weaken the supporting evidence
beats.reason: Handwritten notes do not weaken the supporting evidence. Clear and strongly reasoned enough to persuade or withstand objection.

chains.feedback_short: Handwritten notes do not weaken the supporting evidence.
chains.feedback_deep: Cogent means clear and strongly reasoned enough to persuade or withstand objection; coherent means logically connected and easy to understand, without necessarily being convincing. Here, comparative figures justify the proposed change. The new detail does not change the deciding fact: handwritten notes do not weaken the supporting evidence. Thus cogent remains the stronger choice.
chains.contrast_rule: Coherent is easy to follow; cogent gives strong reasons to believe.
